newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu puts off naming finance chief.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu puts off naming finance chief.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday put off naming a new finance minister while his government struggled to avoid embarrassment in a parliamentary no-confidence motion.

Netanyahu offered hardliner Ariel Sharon the post during a meeting on Tuesday but the former general demanded he also get a top security job for the first time since he was forced out as defence minister over a 1982 massacre of Palestinians.
"The prime minister is dealing with the matter. No appointments will be made today," said an official in the prime minister's office.

The announcement came as 14 of the 66 legislators in Netanyahu's own coalition threatened to abstain or absent themselves from the vote in the 120-member parliament, expected back at around 10:00 p.m. (1900 GMT).

Sharon, 69, insisted Netanyahu let him join Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai and Foreign Minister David Levy in making up the Israeli leader's team of insiders who hammer out strategy in Arab-Israeli negotiations.
"I stated (to Netanyahu) in a very clear fashion that I have to be on this team...that deals with political security issues," Sharon, of Netanyahu's Likud party, told Israel Radio.
The two men failed to resolve the issue at the meeting but agreed to discuss it again on Tuesday or Wednesday.
Political analysts said the burly ex-general was sure to get the post -- a move likely to alarm the Arab world and the United States, Israel's closest ally.

Analysts said Levy and Mordechai, relative moderates in the rightist-religious government, were worried the appointment would yank the cabinet rightward at a time of rising tensions with the PLO over a three-month-old freeze in peace moves.

"This is something devastating for David Levy and Yitzhak Mordechai because they never wanted to share strategy and ideas with Sharon," Shimon Shiffer of the Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper said. "For the Americans and Palestinians, it's very scary."

The opposition was seen as unlikely to muster the 61 votes required to force new elections for parliament and prime minister but a large number of defections by ruling coalition members could signal Netanyahu's year-old government is in trouble.
Five Likud lawmakers were expected to abstain or absent themselves from the vote and five legislators from the Likud-allied Gesher faction headed by Levy were also expected to abstain.

Another four coalition members of the Third Way party said they would also abstain unless Netanyahu distanced himself from remarks Justice Minister Tzachi Hanegbi made against opposition leader Ehud Barak during the no-confidence debate.
Hanegbi caused a political storm by accusing Barak, leader of the Labour party and former army chief, of abandoning wounded soldiers during a 1992 training accident.
"We will not support the government in the no-confidence motion if the prime minister doesn't distance himself from the statements," said Third Way legislator Alex Lubolsky.
Dan Meridor, Netanyahu's Likud rival, was forced out as finance minister last week in a struggle over currency reform.

Sharon's appointment would mark a stunning political comeback since he was forced to quit as defence minister in 1983 after a state inquiry found him indirectly responsible for the killing of hundreds of Palestinians by Lebanese Christians at two Beirut refugee camps encircled by Israeli troops.
The finance post would give Sharon influence in decisions on expanding Jewish settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank and Gaza.
Sharon -- nicknamed "the bulldozer" -- as housing minister in the early 1990s engineered a settlement boom that put Israel on a collision course with the United States.
